title: The optimum is always at a corner
intro: Why a region with infinitely many points has only finitely many candidates.

steps.title: Corners are enough
steps.body:
`Z = ax + by` has a constant gradient, so its contours are parallel lines sweeping across the feasible region. Push the sweep as far as the walls allow and the last point of contact is a **vertex** — or, in the tie case, an edge whose endpoints are vertices anyway.

That is the corner-point theorem, and it is why LP is tractable: infinitely many feasible points, finitely many corners, and the optimum guaranteed to be among them. Enumerating corners is a complete method, not an approximation.

steps.title: A worked allocation
steps.body:
Maximise `Z = 30x + 50y` subject to `x + 2y ≤ 40`, `3x + y ≤ 60`, `x, y ≥ 0` — splitting watts between a CPU and an NPU under a power budget and a thermal ceiling.

| Vertex | Z |
|---|---|
| (0, 0) | 0 |
| (20, 0) | 600 |
| (0, 20) | 1000 |
| **(16, 12)** | **1080** |

The winner sits where the two constraints **cross** — both binding, both resources fully spent. That is the usual shape of an LP answer, and it has a reading: at the optimum you have generally run out of more than one thing at once.

points.label: Interior
points.note: Never optimal — something is unspent and you can still move along the gradient.

points.label: Edge
points.note: Better, but unless the objective is parallel to it you can still slide to a corner.

points.label: Vertex (16, 12)
points.note: Z = 1080. Both constraints binding: power budget and thermal ceiling exhausted together.

steps.title: The trap that ships
steps.body:
`scipy.optimize.linprog` **minimises**. Always. There is no maximise flag.

To maximise you pass `−c`, solve, then **negate the returned value** to recover max Z. Skip the negation and you get the right vertex with a sign error. Skip the `−c` entirely and it is far worse: you get the **minimum** — a perfectly valid-looking point, usually where you have allocated almost nothing — with no exception and no warning. A confident answer to the opposite question.

The defence is the corner table: enumerate the vertices, evaluate Z by hand, and confirm the solver's answer is the best of them. A sign inversion shows up instantly, because the 'optimum' will be sitting at the worst corner in your table.

recap: The feasible region is convex, so the optimum is at a vertex and the corner table is a complete check. The binding constraints at that vertex tell you what you ran out of. And because the library minimises, maximising is a two-step inversion — with a corner table as the cheap way to catch getting it wrong.
